deck: ES2240F Catastrophic Events::Week 2::Ch3 Plumes and Hot Spots

fields.Front: Why is Hawaii important to plate tectonic theory?
fields.Back: The Hawaiian Islands sit in the middle of the Pacific Plate with no plate boundary anywhere close, yet magma erupts every few days or weeks and has done for many millions of years - which needs a stationary, 'blow-torch'-like magma source (a mantle plume) beneath a moving plate.

fields.Front: Describe the Hawaii-Emperor chain and its 'dog-leg'.
fields.Back: A chain of volcanic islands and seamounts whose ages increase away from Hawaii, formed as the Pacific Plate moved over a stationary hot spot. About 43 million years ago the plate shifted direction a bit, making the 'dog-leg' bend in the track (about 60 Myr at the northern Emperor Seamounts, 43 Myr at the bend, 25 and 2-3 Myr along the Hawaiian Ridge).

fields.Front: List the four proofs of the Hawaiian hot-spot theory.
fields.Back:
1) All volcanic islands/seamounts further north than the big island are volcanically dead.
2) On the big island volcanic activity increases toward the southern boundary.
3) A new volcanic mound (Loihi) is rapidly building from the sea floor off the south coast.
4) A tightly defined great plume of heat (hot spot) lies beneath the big island and Loihi.

fields.Front: Define mantle plume and hot spot.
fields.Back: Mantle plume: the great column of hot material rising from deep in the mantle. Hot spot: the top of a plume, where basalt magma forms beneath the lithosphere. Not every hot spot signifies a mantle plume beneath it.

At the core-mantle boundary, from a discontinuous zone called the Ultra Low Velocity Zone (so named because seismic shock waves lose velocity there), which appears to be characterized by very large reservoirs of magma.

fields.Front: How long does plume material take to rise, how long do plumes last, and why do they rise?
fields.Back: Perhaps a couple of million years to rise and push against the brittle lithosphere; plumes exist for 100-200 million years on average. They rise because molten rock almost always has a lower density than solid rock (slides).

fields.Front: What happens when a mantle plume rises under lithosphere?
fields.Back: The lithosphere is a significant barrier, so plume material may spread widely beneath it before finding a zone of weakness and breaking through as a very active volcano. The magma bulges the lithosphere into a DOME; eventually the dome breaks, magma flows out, and the new rift(s) may infill with seawater - as in Eastern Africa today.
When crust of uniform strength in all directions is stressed by rising magma from an underlying hot spot, it breaks into three equally spaced segments - a triple junction.

fields.Front: Give the Red Sea example of a triple junction.
fields.Back: A hot spot sits at the intersection of the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the East African Rift. The Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden are the growing arms and are widening every year; the East African Rift is the failed arm (aulacogen).

fields.Front: How do plumes produce a spreading centre such as the Atlantic?
fields.Back: Given any weakness, brittle crust breaks under the never-ceasing stress from below. Divergent arms from one hot spot connect with arms of adjacent hot spots, and a whole spreading centre is born.

fields.Front: What does Figure 20 show about the life of a hot-spot volcano?
fields.Back: The evolution of an active volcanic island into eroded islands and then seamounts, as the moving plate carries each volcano away from the stationary hot spot and erosion wears it down to and below sea level.

fields.Text: A {{c1::seamount}} is a volcanic island that has been worn down to sea level by {{c1::erosion}}.

The Hawaii-Emperor chain bends because the Pacific Plate changed direction about {{c1::43}} million years ago; the new volcanic mound building off Hawaii's south coast will be called {{c1::Loihi}} when it breaks sea level.

Mantle plumes originate at the {{c1::core-mantle boundary}} in the {{c1::Ultra Low Velocity Zone}}, take about {{c1::a couple of million}} years to reach the lithosphere, and last {{c1::100-200}} million years on average.

A {{c1::superplume}} is an enormously large mantle plume; {{c1::Africa}} is thought to sit over one - a concentration of hot spots connects to it, which may explain why Africa sits at a {{c1::higher elevation}} than its composition warrants.

The magma formed at a hot spot is {{c1::basalt}} (density about {{c1::2.5}} g/cm3); continental lithosphere averages {{c1::2.7}} g/cm3 and oceanic lithosphere about {{c1::3.0}} g/cm3, so the magma rises through either.

An {{c1::aulacogen}} is the {{c1::failed}} arm of a triple junction - the fracture that does not continue to grow (e.g. the {{c1::East African Rift}}) - and remains a region of high {{c1::tectonic instability}}.
A hot spot cracks uniform crust into a {{c1::triple junction}}; commonly only {{c1::two}} arms grow and the failed arm is called an {{c1::aulacogen}}.
A {{c1::hot spot}} is the top of a {{c1::mantle plume}}, where {{c1::basalt}} magma forms - but not every hot spot signifies a {{c1::plume}} beneath it.

Plumes can arise {{c1::anywhere}}, under any kind of surface; where a plume spreads beneath thick, insulating {{c1::continental}} crust, any point of {{c1::weakness}} gives a connection to the magma 'pond' beneath - the model proposed for {{c1::Africa}}.
